title: Chemokine Names, Receptors and Measuring Soluble Immune Signals
summary: Learn how chemokine subfamilies and receptors are named from their cysteine spacing, what bioassays, ELISA and multiplex panels actually measure for cytokines, and why soluble P-selectin is a plasma immunoassay marker rather than a platelet count.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 49 Hits 3 and 4 and Traps 3 and 5, checked against Hughes and Nibbs 2018 and Xavier 2025 (full text via Europe PMC), and Bachelerie 2014, Stenken 2015, Leng 2008 and Ramacciotti 2011 (read via a page-fetch tool). Qualifications recorded: XC chemokines lack the first and third cysteines of the four-cysteine motif; receptors are named for the predominant subfamily they bind and the four atypical receptors do not signal like conventional GPCRs; no source read calls the bioassay the “gold standard” or gives its cost; soluble P-selectin did not outperform D-dimer in a 2025 study. Not taught: the Number Vault (Table 1), Hits 9 and 12, and the chapter figure.

objectives: Classify a chemokine as CC, CXC, CX3C or XC from its cysteine spacing and decode its systematic name.
Describe chemokine receptors as seven-transmembrane GPCRs, their naming, and the atypical-receptor exception.
Contrast what cytokine bioassays, ELISA and multiplex panels measure, and explain how soluble P-selectin is measured and how it performs for DVT.

scenes.title: Three requests at the immunology bench
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three items reach the immunology bench — (1) a research panel report listing CXCL8, CCL2 and CX3CL1; (2) a clinician who has a plasma IL-6 result by ELISA and asks whether the IL-6 is “biologically active”; (3) a request for soluble P-selectin in a patient with suspected deep vein thrombosis (DVT), with a note “or just use the platelet count?”. Question token: “What does each name and number really mean?”

cues.text: Three items reach the immunology bench. A research panel lists CXCL8, CCL2 and CX3CL1. What do those letters mean?

A clinician has an interleukin-6 result by ELISA and asks whether that interleukin-6 is biologically active. And a request for soluble P-selectin arrives for a suspected deep vein thrombosis, with a note: or just use the platelet count?
What does each name, and each number, really mean?

props.label: What does each name and number mean?

scenes.title: Chemokine names spell the cysteines
scenes.altText: Schematic: four short chains, each showing the two cysteines closest to the N terminus. CC: the cysteines sit side by side. CXC: one variable amino acid (X) between them. CX3C: three amino acids between them; only one human member, CX3CL1 (fractalkine). XC: lacks the first and third cysteines of the usual four-cysteine motif; two forms in humans. Name card: subfamily + L (ligand) + number in order of gene isolation, a systematic nomenclature introduced in 2000.

cues.text: Chemokines are grouped by the two cysteines closest to their N terminus. In CC chemokines those two cysteines sit side by side.
In CXC chemokines one variable amino acid, the X, sits between them. The single CX3C chemokine has three amino acids between them: CX3CL1, also called fractalkine.
XC chemokines lack the first and the third cysteines of the usual four-cysteine motif. Humans have two forms.

The systematic names, introduced in 2000, read like a spelling: the subfamily, then L for ligand, then a number in the order the gene was first isolated. So CXCL8 is CXC ligand number 8 in that order.

scenes.title: Receptors take the same letters
scenes.altText: Receptor card: chemokine receptors are heptahelical (seven-transmembrane) G protein-coupled receptors. Conventional receptors signal through pertussis toxin-sensitive Gαi proteins and β-arrestins, leading to migration and adhesion. Names: predominant subfamily bound + R + number in order of discovery; 18 conventional receptors: 10 CCR, 6 CXCR, 1 CX3CR (CX3CR1, the fractalkine receptor), 1 XCR. Exception card: four atypical chemokine receptors (ACKR1–4) are structurally related but do not couple to many, if any, of those pathways; several act as scavengers. Promiscuity card: many chemokines bind several receptors and some receptors have many ligands. Tether card: CX3CL1 and CXCL16 have a mucin-like stalk and transmembrane domain that hold them on the cell surface; the stalk can be cleaved to release the chemokine.

cues.text: Chemokine receptors are seven-transmembrane, G protein-coupled receptors. Conventional receptors signal through pertussis toxin-sensitive G-alpha-i proteins and beta-arrestins, and the cell moves or adheres.
They are named for the main subfamily they bind, then R for receptor, then a number in order of discovery: ten CCRs, six CXCRs, one CX3CR and one XCR.
The exception: four atypical chemokine receptors, ACKR1 to ACKR4, look similar but do not couple to many, if any, of those signalling pathways. Several act as scavengers that remove chemokines.
And the network is promiscuous: many chemokines bind several receptors. Two chemokines, CX3CL1 and CXCL16, are even anchored on the cell surface by a stalk that can be cut to release them.

scenes.title: Measuring soluble signals
scenes.altText: Assay cards. Bioassay: measures active cytokine through a biological outcome (for example cell proliferation); distinguishes active from inactive forms; slow, and far fewer are available. Immunoassay (ELISA): the standard method; antibody binding to the cytokine protein; one cytokine per well, about 100 µL of sample; cytokine bound to its soluble receptor typically cannot be quantified. Multiplex bead (Luminex) and electrochemiluminescence (Meso Scale) panels: many cytokines at once, less sample, wider range (3–4 logs vs 1–2 for ELISA), but large inter-laboratory variation; ELISA–multiplex agreement is weaker in serum and plasma. Soluble P-selectin card: stored in platelet α-granules and endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies, partly released in soluble form on activation, measured by ELISA on citrated plasma — not a CBC parameter; at 90 ng/mL one study found 28% sensitivity and 96% specificity; a 2025 study found AUC 0.70–0.77, below D-dimer at 0.92. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Cytokines circulate at picogram-per-millilitre levels. A bioassay measures active cytokine through a biological effect, such as cell proliferation, so it can tell active from inactive forms. But bioassays are slow, and far fewer exist.

Immunoassays are the standard methods. An ELISA measures one cytokine per well by antibody binding, and cytokine bound to a soluble receptor is typically missed. Multiplex bead and electrochemiluminescence panels measure many at once, but vary more between laboratories and agree less well with ELISA in serum and plasma.

Soluble P-selectin is shed from activated platelets and endothelium, and is measured by ELISA on plasma, not counted on a blood count. As a deep vein thrombosis marker, a 2025 study found it did not outperform D-dimer.
Back to the hook. The names spell cysteine spacing; the ELISA gives protein, not activity; and suspected thrombosis still goes to pretest probability, D-dimer and imaging.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “CXC means two adjacent cysteines” (✓ CC = adjacent; CXC = one amino acid between); “An ELISA result shows biological activity” (✓ an immunoassay measures the protein; only a bioassay separates active from inactive forms); “Soluble P-selectin is read from the platelet count” (✓ it is a plasma immunoassay, and in a 2025 study it did not beat D-dimer).

cues.text: Trap one: CXC means two cysteines side by side. No: side by side is CC. In CXC one amino acid sits between them.
Trap two: an ELISA result shows biological activity. No: an immunoassay measures the protein. Only a bioassay separates active from inactive forms.
Trap three: soluble P-selectin comes from the platelet count. No: it is a plasma immunoassay, and in a 2025 study it did not beat D-dimer.

scenes.title: Read the name, weigh the key
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Read the name like a spelling — C is a cysteine, X is a spacer, the 3 counts spacers, L is ligand, R is receptor, the number is the order of discovery. Then remember: ELISA weighs the key; the bioassay turns it in the lock.” Tokens: C = cysteine · X = spacer · L/R = ligand/receptor · ELISA = weigh · bioassay = turn. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: read the name like a spelling. C is a cysteine, X is a spacer, the three counts spacers, L is ligand, R is receptor, and the number is only the order of discovery. Then: the ELISA weighs the key, but the bioassay turns it in the lock.

Where it breaks: XC chemokines lack two of the four cysteines, not just one letter; receptors are named for the main subfamily they bind, yet many bind several chemokines and atypical receptors barely signal; and an ELISA can miss cytokine hidden on its receptor.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “CC adjacent · CXC one between · CX3C three between · XC missing cysteines; ligand L, receptor R”, “ELISA = protein · bioassay = activity · soluble P-selectin = plasma immunoassay, not better than D-dimer”.

cues.text: Chemokine and receptor names spell out cysteine spacing, an ELISA measures cytokine protein while only a bioassay measures activity, and soluble P-selectin is a plasma immunoassay marker that has not outperformed D-dimer for deep vein thrombosis.

props.label: CC · CXC · CX3C · XC = cysteine spacing; L ligand, R receptor
ELISA = protein · bioassay = activity · sP-selectin ≠ CBC

explanation.what: Plain language: chemokines are small attractant proteins whose family names describe where two key cysteines sit; their receptors borrow the same letters. Measuring these signals is a separate question: antibody tests count the protein, while a bioassay checks whether it still works. Scientific terms: CC, CXC, CX3C and XC subfamilies; systematic L (ligand) and R (receptor) nomenclature; seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptor; Gαi and β-arrestin signalling; atypical chemokine receptors (ACKR1–4); fractalkine (CX3CL1); bioassay; enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA); multiplex bead and electrochemiluminescence immunoassays; soluble P-selectin; area under the ROC curve (AUC).
explanation.why: Cysteine spacing is the structural basis of the chemokine families, and the naming system encodes it. Cytokines are low-abundance (pg/mL) proteins; antibody-based assays detect the protein but cannot tell active from inactive forms and may miss cytokine bound to soluble receptors. P-selectin is stored in platelet α-granules and endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies and partly released into plasma on activation, so it is measured as a soluble protein.
explanation.measure: CC: adjacent cysteines; CXC: one amino acid between; CX3C: three between (CX3CL1 only); XC: lacks the first and third of four cysteines. 18 conventional receptors: 10 CCR, 6 CXCR, 1 CX3CR, 1 XCR; 4 ACKRs. ELISA: one cytokine per well, about 100 µL sample, 1–2 logs of range; bead multiplex: 3–4 logs, many analytes, larger inter-laboratory variation. Soluble P-selectin by ELISA on citrated plasma; at 90 ng/mL, 28% sensitivity and 96% specificity (Ramacciotti 2011); AUC 0.70–0.77 vs D-dimer 0.92 in merged cohorts (Xavier 2025).
explanation.differs: CC vs CXC vs CX3C vs XC; conventional receptors (signal, drive migration) vs atypical receptors (little or no G-protein signalling, scavenging); bioassay (activity) vs immunoassay (protein); soluble P-selectin (plasma immunoassay) vs platelet count (CBC).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the subfamily from a cysteine pattern or a name such as CX3CL1, recognise the receptor class, choose the assay that measures biological activity, or reject the idea that soluble P-selectin is a CBC parameter or a replacement for D-dimer.

mnemonic.text: Read the name like a spelling — C is a cysteine, X is a spacer, the 3 counts spacers, L is ligand, R is receptor, the number is the order of discovery. ELISA weighs the key; the bioassay turns it in the lock.
mnemonic.explanation: Decodes chemokine and receptor names and separates protein measurement from activity measurement.
mnemonic.limitation: XC chemokines lack two of the four conserved cysteines, not just one letter; receptors are named for the predominant subfamily they bind, binding is promiscuous and atypical receptors barely signal; an ELISA can miss cytokine bound to a soluble receptor.

analogyLimitations: Chemokine chains are schematic, not structures.
Diagnostic accuracy figures come from single studies with their own assays and cut-offs.
takeaway: Chemokine and receptor names spell out cysteine spacing, an ELISA measures cytokine protein while only a bioassay measures activity, and soluble P-selectin is a plasma immunoassay marker that has not outperformed D-dimer for deep vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: A chemokine has exactly one amino acid between the two cysteines closest to its N terminus. To which subfamily does it belong, and how are its receptors named?

options.text: CXC; its receptors are named CXCR
options.rationale: Correct. One variable amino acid (X) between the cysteines defines CXC, and conventional receptors are named for the subfamily they predominantly bind plus R.

options.text: CC; its receptors are named CCR
options.rationale: Incorrect. In CC chemokines the two cysteines are directly adjacent.
Incorrect. CX3C has three amino acids between the cysteines, and its only member is CX3CL1 (fractalkine).
Incorrect. XC chemokines lack the first and third cysteines of the four-cysteine motif.

questions.stem: A plasma IL-6 result was produced by ELISA. The clinician asks whether the IL-6 measured is biologically active. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The ELISA measures IL-6 protein by antibody binding; a bioassay is needed to separate active from inactive forms
options.rationale: Correct. Bioassays measure active cytokine through a biological outcome; immunoassays measure the protein.

options.text: The ELISA measures activity, because the antibodies bind only active IL-6
options.rationale: Incorrect. Immunoassays do not establish activity, and cytokine bound to a soluble receptor is typically missed.

options.text: A multiplex bead panel would report activity instead
options.rationale: Incorrect. Bead and electrochemiluminescence panels are also immunoassays; they add analytes, not activity.

options.text: Bioassays are the fastest and most widely available cytokine tests
options.rationale: Incorrect. Bioassays take a long time and far fewer are available; immunoassays are the standard methods.

questions.stem: A request asks for soluble P-selectin in a patient with suspected deep vein thrombosis. Which statement is best supported?

options.text: It is measured by immunoassay on plasma, and in a 2025 study it did not outperform D-dimer
options.rationale: Correct. Studies measured it by ELISA on plasma; total P-selectin had an AUC of 0.70–0.77 versus 0.92 for D-dimer.

options.text: It is calculated from the platelet count on the CBC
options.rationale: Incorrect. It is a soluble protein shed from activated platelets and endothelium, not a CBC parameter.

options.text: It has replaced D-dimer in the guideline rule-out pathway
options.rationale: Incorrect. Guidelines use pretest probability with D-dimer, then imaging; a 2025 study concluded P-selectin could not replace or supplement D-dimer.

options.text: It comes only from leukocytes rolling on the vessel wall
options.rationale: Incorrect. P-selectin is stored in platelet α-granules and endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies.

claims.text: CC, CXC, CX3C and XC defined by N-terminal cysteine spacing; CX3CL1 (fractalkine) sole CX3C; XC lacks first and third cysteines; L/number nomenclature.

Chemokine receptors are seven-transmembrane GPCRs signalling via Gαi and β-arrestins; named by predominant subfamily + R + number; 10 CCR, 6 CXCR, 1 CX3CR, 1 XCR; promiscuous binding; CX3CL1 and CXCL16 membrane-tethered.
Four atypical chemokine receptors do not couple to many if any conventional pathways; several scavenge chemokines.

Bioassay measures activity and separates active from inactive forms but is slow and scarce; immunoassays are standard; ELISA limits; multiplex range and reproducibility; weaker ELISA–multiplex agreement in serum/plasma; pg/mL concentrations.

Soluble P-selectin: platelet α-granule and Weibel–Palade body origin, plasma ELISA, 28%/96% at 90 ng/mL, AUC 0.70–0.77 vs D-dimer 0.92; guideline pathway uses pretest probability, D-dimer and imaging.
Bioassay described as the “gold standard” for cytokine activity; bioassay cost and hospital manageability; chemokine molecular weight 8–14 kDa.
claims.note: Not taught; no source read in this session supports these.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 49 Hit 3 says XC chemokines lack “the first cysteine”. Hughes and Nibbs 2018: XC chemokines lack the first and the third cysteines of the conserved four-cysteine motif (register flag rv-xc-chemokine-cysteines).

Ch. 49 Hit 4 says chemokine receptors are 7-transmembrane GPCRs named for the subclass they bind. Hughes and Nibbs 2018 and Bachelerie 2014: conventional receptors are named for the predominant subfamily bound and binding is promiscuous; the four atypical receptors (ACKR1–4) are structurally related but do not couple to many, if any, G-protein pathways (register flag rv-atypical-chemokine-receptors).

Ch. 49 Trap 3 calls the bioassay the “gold standard” for cytokine activity and “too slow and costly” for hospitals. Stenken 2015 supports that bioassays measure activity, discriminate active from inactive forms, take long and are few, but neither it nor Leng 2008 calls them a gold standard or addresses cost (register flag rv-cytokine-bioassay-gold-standard).

Ch. 49 Trap 5 presents soluble P-selectin as a DVT biomarker. Xavier 2025: total plasma P-selectin had moderate accuracy (AUC 0.70–0.77), inferior to D-dimer alone (AUC 0.92), and adding it did not improve D-dimer; guidelines rely on pretest probability, D-dimer and imaging (register flag rv-soluble-p-selectin-dvt).
